key_idea: Swapping two entries of Q multiplies P=H∘Q by a transposition: the cycle count goes up by one if the two positions were in the same cycle and down by one otherwise. Keep a set of representatives known to be in distinct cycles; merging a subset of them changes the count predictably, so one query tests whether a new vertex lies in any of those cycles.
sketch: Start from a random Q and learn c = cycles(P). Process vertices in random order: binary search over the current representatives (plus the outcome 'new cycle') by chaining swaps among a block of representatives and then swapping with the new vertex; the reply is c-cnt+2 if it is inside the block and c-cnt otherwise. If it shares a cycle with representative r, permanently swap Q[a],Q[r], splitting them (c++); either way a becomes a representative. When all N are representatives P is the identity, so H = Q^{-1}, submitted as the last query. Outcomes are in bijection with permutations, so with a random start each search is uniform and the total is about log2(N!) + small, around 1410-1430 for N=220, versus the 1537 worst case of a deterministic order; the non-adaptive judge makes the randomisation safe. Pitfalls: stop on 0 at any point, skip 'new cycle' when every cycle already has a representative. Interactive: verified with my own local judge simulator (max 1428 queries over 40 runs at N=220 including identity and one big cycle), not by the sample checker.
